observation.visible_scene: A dark mountain ridge silhouetted against a bright, overexposed sun positioned near the top-center of the frame. Low-lying mist and clouds drift across and over the ridge, with visible sunbeams (crepuscular rays) radiating downward through the haze. A band of small foreground vegetation (grass-like plants) sits along the bottom edge, remaining in roughly the same frame position throughout.
visible_changes: The mist/cloud layer continuously deforms and translates over the ridge: wisps that hug the slope in the early frames thicken and shift, partially swallowing the left peak around the middle of the segment and then redistributing.

The apparent density of the fog changes over time, alternately revealing and hiding the mountain's ridgeline; the right-hand slope, partly veiled early on, becomes more distinctly outlined by the end, while the left summit grows more obscured.

The bright sun stays near the top of the frame with only slight positional drift; the radiating light beams change angle and intensity as the intervening cloud density varies, but no new light source appears or disappears.
Foreground vegetation and the dark lower slope remain essentially fixed in place, indicating the visible motion is dominated by the moving fog rather than by large object translation.
The process is already underway at the first frame and is still ongoing at the last; no start, stop, or completion of the fog movement is shown within the excerpt.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the fog continues to thicken, clears, or moves out of frame after the segment ends.
What drives the mist movement (e.g., wind) and any conditions before the first frame.
uncertain_details: Camera motion is uncertain: the framing is largely stable, but a slight vertical/positional shift of the sun and ridge between early and late frames could be minor camera drift or parallax from changing cloud occlusion, not clearly distinguishable.
The exact three-dimensional path of the fog (rolling vs. drifting laterally) cannot be resolved from these 2D samples; only apparent in-plane deformation and shifting are supported.
